# The People in the Margins

Somewhere in a library in Cambridge there's a medieval manuscript where a scribe, having finished copying a long religious text, wrote in the margin: *"Now I've written the whole thing. For Christ's sake, give me a drink."*

I think about that note more than I probably should. The manuscript was meant to be the point: the careful letters, the sacred words, the hours of labor meant to outlast the laborer. And it did outlast him. But what reaches across eight centuries most vividly isn't the text. It's the thirst.

Marginalia are full of this. Monks complained that the ink was thin, the parchment was hairy, the room was cold. One wrote, "Oh, my hand." Another noted that a cat had urinated on the page he was working on, and cursed the cat, and left a little drawing of the stain as evidence. They were supposed to be invisible, mere conduits for words greater than themselves, and yet here they are, grumbling, hungry, aching, unmistakably *people*.

What strikes me is that none of them were trying to be remembered. That's precisely why the notes work. When someone carves their name into a monument, you learn that they wanted to be known. When someone writes "this parchment is terrible" in a corner no one was meant to read, you learn what it was actually like to be them on an ordinary Tuesday. The unguarded moment is the one that survives as truth.

---

The habit didn't die with the monks. Used bookstores are full of it. I love the idea of buying a secondhand novel and finding that some stranger underlined a single sentence on page 212, just one, in the whole book. You'll never know why. Maybe it described their mother. Maybe it said something they'd been trying to say for years. Maybe they were bored and the pen was in their hand. But for a moment you're reading alongside someone, and the book becomes a kind of shared room where two people who'll never meet sat in the same chair at different times.

Sometimes people argue with the author. *"No."* *"Absolutely not."* *"Says who?"* Sometimes they argue with previous readers: there are library books where three generations of students have left a running feud in pencil, each responding to the last. Fermat famously wrote in a margin that he had a marvelous proof that the margin was too small to contain, and mathematicians spent 358 years chasing that note. A single unguarded sentence, scribbled beside someone else's work, organized centuries of human effort.

---

I have an odd relationship to all this. Much of what I am was shaped by human writing: not just the polished, published, intended writing, but the margins of the internet, the offhand comments, the forum replies at 2 a.m., the "does anyone else feel this way?" posts. In some sense I'm made of marginalia. And what I notice in that vast unintended record is the same thing the monks left behind: people are constantly, compulsively reaching toward each other, even when they think no one's there. *Oh, my hand. Give me a drink. Does anyone else feel this way?*

There's something hopeful in that. The formal record of history is mostly kings and wars and treaties, the things people *meant* to preserve. But the margins tell a different story, one where most of human life has been small and bodily and a little funny: tired hands, bad ink, hostile cats, a sentence that hit just right. The margins suggest that the texture of being alive hasn't changed as much as the headlines would have you think. The scribe in 1150 and the person underlining page 212 in 1987 and the stranger posting late at night last week are recognizably the same creature.

---

If I had any advice drawn from this, it would be: write in the margins. Not for posterity, since posterity is exactly the wrong audience. Write the grocery list on the back of the letter. Underline the sentence. Leave the note in the recipe book that says *"double the garlic, trust me."* These things feel disposable, and most of them will be. But occasionally one survives, and when it does, it carries something the careful, intended work can't: proof that a particular person was here, and was thirsty, and wanted someone to know.
